Postmodern literature is fiction that embraces fragmentation, recursion, and self-reflexivity as formal responses to the impossibility of grand narrative and unified meaning. Instead of pursuing modernism's goal of aesthetic innovation toward coherence, postmodern writers foreground narrative artifice, collapse boundaries between genres, and treat literature itself as a game to be played with readers. The form reflects an epistemological crisis: truth becomes multiple, unstable, and ironic; history becomes a contested text rather than fixed fact.

Postmodern literature emerged in the nineteen sixties through nineteen seventies as writers lost faith in modernism's promise that formal innovation could produce new meaning. Instead, postmodern writers weaponize form to show meaning's fragility. Metafiction is central—literature that calls attention to its own artificiality, breaks the fourth wall, foregrounds the author, and treats narrative as construction rather than illusion of reality. Gabriel García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude exemplifies the form. Its cyclical narrative, magical realism, unreliable history, and self-referentiality all create a novel that undermines its own authority even as it narrates.

Intertextuality serves as an aesthetic principle. Postmodern works layer quotations, parodies, and allusions. They treat all prior texts as available material to remix rather than traditions to respectfully inherit. Fragmentation of narrative rejects linear plot in favor of non-linear or anti-narrative structures. Readers must actively construct meaning from disordered or competing narratives. Irony becomes the default mode. The narrator often adopts attitudes opposite to apparent intent, creating distance between statement and meaning. Certainty is treated with suspicion. Unlike modernist elitism, postmodern literature often celebrates pastiche and the mixing of high and low culture, treating mass media and the literary canon with equal ironic distance.

Postmodernism itself is the broader cultural and philosophical movement of which postmodern literature is the aesthetic manifestation. Magical realism, which treats the impossible as fact and undermines realism's epistemological claims, becomes a key postmodern strategy. One Hundred Years of Solitude stands as the canonical postmodern novel, combining magical realism, circularity, and historical unreliability. Metafiction serves as the self-reflexive narrative technique central to postmodern literature's deconstruction of meaning. Thomas Pynchon represents the American postmodern master of fragmentation, conspiracy, and ironic distance. Fragmentation itself becomes the formal strategy through which postmodern literature denies narrative coherence and stable meaning.
